title: Localization of simplicial spaces and the cartesian interval criterion
statement:
Use the Reedy model category, mapping simplicial sets $\operatorname{Map}$, representables $F(n)$ and cartesian internal hom from [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian], with the model-category axioms of [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. Let $f:P\hookrightarrow Q$ be a monomorphism of small simplicial spaces. An $f$-local object means a Reedy fibrant simplicial space $W$ for which $\operatorname{Map}(Q,W)\to\operatorname{Map}(P,W)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Call $g:A\to B$ an $f$-local equivalence if $\operatorname{Map}(B,W)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,W)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every $f$-local object $W$.

There is a model structure on small simplicial spaces with monomorphisms as cofibrations, $f$-local equivalences as weak equivalences, and $f$-local objects as fibrant objects. It is simplicial for $\operatorname{Map}$: for a monomorphism $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ and a fibration $p:X\to Y$ of this structure, the map $\operatorname{Map}(B,X)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,X)\times_{\operatorname{Map}(A,Y)}\operatorname{Map}(B,Y)$ is a Kan fibration in the sense of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], trivial if $i$ is an $f$-local equivalence or $p$ is an $f$-local equivalence. Its fibrations are the maps having the right lifting property against all monomorphisms that are $f$-local equivalences. Every Reedy weak equivalence is an $f$-local equivalence.

Assume, in addition, that $W^{F(1)}$ is $f$-local for every $f$-local object $W$. Then for monomorphisms $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ and $j:C\hookrightarrow D$, their cartesian pushout product
$$(A\times D)\amalg_{A\times C}(B\times C)\longrightarrow B\times D$$
is an $f$-local equivalence whenever either $i$ or $j$ is an $f$-local equivalence.

source.place: Rezk, A model for the homotopy theory of homotopy theory, Propositions 9.1 and 9.2, printed pp. 21-22; cartesian compatibility is interpreted by Section 2.5(1). Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this simplicial-space result.

proof.text: Write $C$ for monomorphisms, $W_f$ for the mapping-test equivalences in the statement, and $T=C\cap W_f$. Every object is Reedy cofibrant since its initial map is a monomorphism. For a Reedy fibrant local $Z$, the Reedy mapping axiom makes $\operatorname{Map}(i,Z)$ a Kan fibration for every $i\in C$, hence a trivial Kan fibration exactly when $i\in W_f$. Every Reedy weak equivalence $g$ belongs to $W_f$: factor $g=ba$ with $a$ a Reedy trivial cofibration and $b$ a Reedy trivial fibration. The map $b$ has a section $s$ by cofibrancy of its target. The section is a monomorphism and a Reedy weak equivalence by two-out-of-three, so both $\operatorname{Map}(a,Z)$ and $\operatorname{Map}(s,Z)$ are trivial Kan fibrations. The identity $bs=1$ and two-out-of-three give that $\operatorname{Map}(b,Z)$ is a weak equivalence, hence so is $\operatorname{Map}(g,Z)$. Finally $W_f$ is retract closed and has two-out-of-three, by applying the corresponding Kan weak-equivalence axioms to each mapping test.

source.place: Proposition 9.1(3)-(4); Sections 2.3-2.4 Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: The class $T$ is closed under pushout, small coproducts, transfinite composition and arrow retracts. Monomorphisms have these closure properties degreewise in sets. For a local $Z$, mapping a pushout into $Z$ is a pullback, and mapping a coproduct is a product. Pullbacks and products of trivial Kan fibrations remain trivial: solve each boundary lifting problem by pulling back a filler or choosing a filler in each coordinate. For a continuous ordinal chain of $T$-maps, mapping its colimit into $Z$ is the inverse limit of a tower whose successor maps are trivial Kan fibrations. Given a boundary square for its projection to the first stage, choose compatible simplex fillers at successor stages and use the limit universal property at limit stages. This proves the projection is a trivial Kan fibration. Retracts are handled by composing a boundary square with the section and retraction. These arguments use the boundary-lifting characterization, including degree zero, and establish the claimed closure of $T$ without any homotopy-limit theorem.

source.place: Proposition 9.1 proof, closure needed for the small-object construction Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-simplicial-local-bounded-lifting] to choose $\gamma$ and a set $J=J_\gamma\subseteq T$ with $J^{\square}=T^{\square}$. This is a small set: all its underlying bisimplicial sets can be represented on sets of cardinality less than $\gamma$, with structure maps indexed by the countable category $\Delta\times\Delta$. Choose a small uncountable regular cardinal $\kappa>\gamma$. A map from a domain of $J$ into the colimit of a $\kappa$-chain factors through one stage: there are fewer than $\kappa$ simplices and fewer than $\kappa$ operator equations to place at a common stage, by regularity. The same argument makes two such maps equal at a common stage when they agree in the colimit. Colimits here are computed in sets in each bidegree. Thus the smallness hypothesis of [lem-coef-small-object-cell-factorization] holds. That theorem gives functorial factorizations as a $J$-cell map followed by a member of $F_f:=T^{\square}$. Step 2 puts every $J$-cell map in $T$. Every member of $T$ lifts against every member of $F_f=T^{\square}$ by definition, so $T\subseteq{}^{\square}F_f$. Conversely, let $g$ lift against every member of $F_f$ and factor $g=p_gj_g$ as above; $g$ lifts against $p_g\in F_f$ in the square formed by $1$ and $j_g$, and the filler exhibits $g$ as an arrow retract of $j_g$. Since $j_g\in T$ and $T$ is closed under arrow retracts (Step 2), $g\in T$. (Equivalently: ${}^{\square}F_f={}^{\pitchfork}(J^{\pitchfork})$ is the class of retracts of $J$-cell maps by the cited theorem, which lies in $T$ by Step 2.) Thus $T={}^{\square}F_f$ and $F_f=T^{\square}$, and $(T,F_f)$ is a functorial weak factorization system.

source.place: Proposition 9.1 proof, Bousfield-Smith bound and the small-object argument Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: The old Reedy trivial fibrations are exactly $C^{\square}$, so they lie in $F_f\cap W_f$ by Step 1 and $T\subseteq C$. Conversely, let $p\in F_f\cap W_f$ and factor it in the Reedy model as $p=qi$, where $i\in C$ and $q$ is an old trivial fibration. Step 1 and two-out-of-three imply $i\in T$. The lift of $i$ against $p$ in the factorization square makes $p$ an arrow retract of $q$. Hence $p$ is an old trivial fibration, by the Reedy model axioms. Therefore $F_f\cap W_f=C^{\square}$ and the old functorial factorization supplies $(C,F_f\cap W_f)$. With Step 3 and two-out-of-three and retract closure from Step 1, these are exactly all the model-category axioms. In particular the fibrations are the maps lifting against all monomorphisms in $W_f$.

source.place: Proposition 9.1 proof, model axioms from the two factorizations Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: We verify the simplicial axiom before identifying the new fibrant objects. Denote by $cL$ the constant simplicial space on a simplicial set $L$. For a monomorphism $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ and a horn inclusion $h$, the tensor pushout product $i\mathbin\square ch$ is an old Reedy trivial cofibration: $ch$ is a monomorphism and a levelwise weak equivalence, and the old cartesian pushout-product clause applies. It is in $T$ by Step 1. Tensor-Hom adjunction now transposes every horn lifting square for the mapping-corner map of $(i,p)$, $p\in F_f$, to a square from $i\mathbin\square ch$ against $p$, which has a filler. Thus the mapping corner is Kan. If $i\in T$, then for any simplicial-set monomorphism $j:L\hookrightarrow N$, the arrow $i\mathbin\square cj$ lies in $T$: for a local $Z$ the map $t=\operatorname{Map}(B,Z)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,Z)$ is a trivial Kan fibration by Step 1; mapping $i\mathbin\square cj$ into $Z$ gives the corner of $j$ and $t$. A boundary lifting problem for that corner transposes to a lifting problem from $j\mathbin\square(\partial\Delta^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m)$ against $t$. This pushout product is a monomorphism (the union of two product subobjects), so it lifts by the Kan weak factorization system. The corner is therefore a trivial Kan fibration. Taking $j$ to be each boundary and transposing back proves the mapping-corner map of $(i,p)$ trivial. If instead $p\in F_f\cap W_f$, Step 4 makes it an old trivial fibration and the old simplicial axiom gives triviality. All tensors, cotensors and the enrichment are the original ones, with $A\otimes L=A\times cL$, so this proves the full asserted simplicial model axiom without the interval hypothesis.

source.place: Proposition 9.1, simplicial-model assertion; Sections 2.3-2.5 Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: An old Reedy fibrant local $Z$ is new fibrant: for every $i\in T$, the map $\operatorname{Map}(i,Z)$ is a trivial Kan fibration by Step 1, so its degree-zero surjectivity fills every square from $i$ to $Z\to1$. Conversely a new fibrant $Z$ is old Reedy fibrant since all old trivial cofibrations lie in $T$. The given $f:P\hookrightarrow Q$ itself lies in $T$, directly from the definition of the tests. Step 5 applied to $(f,Z\to1)$ therefore says $\operatorname{Map}(f,Z)$ is a trivial Kan fibration, so $Z$ is local. This identifies the fibrant objects exactly, and completes the first paragraph of the conclusion.

source.place: Proposition 9.1(1)-(4), exact fibrant-object identification Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: Assume now the interval hypothesis. Induction, beginning with $W$ itself at $n=0$, shows $W^{(F(1))^n}$ local: the successor is its exponent by $F(1)$ and exponential currying identifies the two objects. Here is the explicit retract used by Rezk. On ordered sets define $e:[n]\to[1]^n$ by $e(k)_j=1$ if $j\leq k$ and $0$ otherwise, for $1\leq j\leq n$, and define $r:[1]^n\to[n]$ by the sum of the coordinates. Both are monotone and $re=1$. Taking nerves, regarded as discrete simplicial spaces, gives $F(n)\to(F(1))^n\to F(n)$ with composite the identity; in bidegrees these maps just postcompose each monotone simplex with $e$ or $r$. This includes $n=0$, since the empty product and $F(0)$ are terminal. Precomposition makes $W^{F(n)}$ a retract of $W^{(F(1))^n}$. Reedy fibrancy is closed under retracts by the model lifting axiom, and its mapping test is a retract of a weak equivalence, hence a weak equivalence. Thus $W^{F(n)}$ is local for every $n$.

source.place: Proposition 9.2 proof, first paragraph; explicit formula for its elementary retract Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: For any monomorphism $u:A\hookrightarrow B$ and old Reedy fibrant $W$, the restriction $W^B\to W^A$ is an old Reedy fibration. Indeed lifting a Reedy trivial cofibration $v$ against it transposes to lifting $v\mathbin\square u$ against $W\to1$, and the old cartesian pushout-product clause makes $v\mathbin\square u$ Reedy trivial. The same argument with $\varnothing\to X$ shows $W^X$ Reedy fibrant for every $X$. Apply this to $u=f$. By the internal-hom formula, the level-$n$ map of $W^Q\to W^P$ identifies with $\operatorname{Map}(Q,W^{F(n)})\to\operatorname{Map}(P,W^{F(n)})$, which is a weak equivalence by Step 7. The Reedy definition makes this restriction a Reedy weak equivalence as well as a fibration, hence an old trivial fibration. Since every $X$ is cofibrant, the old mapping axiom makes $\operatorname{Map}(X,W^Q)\to\operatorname{Map}(X,W^P)$ a trivial Kan fibration. Currying identifies it with $\operatorname{Map}(Q,W^X)\to\operatorname{Map}(P,W^X)$. Together with Reedy fibrancy of $W^X$ this proves $W^X$ local for every small $X$. This replaces the source's homotopy-colimit/homotopy-limit sentence by a direct Reedy argument.

source.place: Proposition 9.2 proof, middle paragraph; alternate proof below the unit of arbitrary-exponent locality Written argument supplied by Q98; source not archived in literature/.

proof.text: Let $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ and $j:C\hookrightarrow D$ be monomorphisms and suppose $i\in W_f$; symmetry handles the other case. Their cartesian pushout product $k$ is a monomorphism by the old cartesian assertion. Fix a local $W$. In the square obtained by applying $\operatorname{Map}(-,W)$ to the four product objects, its two parallel maps induced by $i$ identify under currying with $\operatorname{Map}(B,W^D)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,W^D)$ and $\operatorname{Map}(B,W^C)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,W^C)$. Step 8 makes the two targets of these mapping tests local, so Step 1 makes both maps trivial Kan fibrations. Put $E=\operatorname{Map}(B\times D,W)$, $U=\operatorname{Map}(A\times D,W)$, $V=\operatorname{Map}(B\times C,W)$ and $H=\operatorname{Map}(A\times C,W)$. The projection $U\times_H V\to U$ is a trivial Kan fibration, being the pullback of $V\to H$; a boundary filler pulls back to give a filler. Its composite with the canonical map $E\to U\times_H V$ is the trivial Kan fibration $E\to U$. Two-out-of-three therefore makes $E\to U\times_H V$ a weak equivalence. The enriched pushout universal property identifies this map exactly with $\operatorname{Map}(k,W)$. Thus $k\in W_f$, proving the final conclusion. This explicit ordinary-pullback calculation requires no unstated homotopy-pullback comparison.
